analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from requiring food safety warnings stricter than federal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House subcommittee before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal food law to stop any state or city from keeping or creating food safety warnings or disclosure rules unless they exactly matched federal standards [S2][S3]. States could have petitioned the federal Health Secretary for an exemption or for a national rule, and could still act in a narrow "imminent hazard" emergency [S2][S3]. In practice, this would have wiped out state-level warning systems — such as California's requirement that foods and products carry warnings about cancer-causing chemicals — and left federal regulators as the only source of food safety warnings. The bill was introduced in August 1998 and never advanced past a House subcommittee [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage manufacturers, packagers, and retailers. Today they must track dozens of state warning and labeling rules; under the bill, one federal standard would replace them all [S2][S3]. Because federal rules are generally weaker and slower to change than state rules, the bill would also have removed state warnings that federal law does not require, reducing labels and notices companies consider costly or reputationally damaging [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food and beverage manufacturers and retailers

how_it_helps.text: Bars any state or locality from enforcing a food safety warning or mandatory disclosure requirement unless it is identical to federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act requirements [S2][S3].
The definition of "notification requirement" reaches every means of communication, including labels, posters, public notices, and advertising [S3].

Gives states a petition process to win an exemption from the federal Health Secretary or to push for a national standard, with deadlines for federal action and court review if the Secretary stalls [S2][S3].
Leaves untouched state rules on freshness dating, open-date labeling, unit pricing, religious dietary labeling, organic designations, and statements of origin [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who would lose state-mandated warnings about hazards in food — for example, warnings required under state right-to-know laws — whenever federal law did not mandate the same notice [S2][S3]. State governments would lose the power to set their own food safety disclosure rules, and would bear the burden of petitioning the federal government for any exception [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Defenders of national uniformity argue a patchwork of state warning rules raises costs for companies selling in all fifty states, and that those costs can be passed to consumers in higher prices; a single federal standard simplifies compliance [S2][S3].

The bill does carve out real state authority: states can still act on "imminent hazards" likely to cause serious health harm or death, can petition for exemptions protecting important public interests, and keep rules on dating, pricing, and origin labels [S2][S3].

The exemption process depends on the federal Health Secretary's judgment, and the bar for an emergency exception — an imminent hazard likely to cause serious consequences or death — is far higher than the ordinary precaution standard states use to require warnings [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: National uniformity has a real logic: companies selling nationwide do face compliance costs from differing state rules. But the cost here falls on the safety side of the ledger. The bill would have replaced the tougher, faster-moving state warning systems with a single federal floor and made every exception dependent on federal approval within tight deadlines [S2][S3]. States would have gone from setting their own standards to petitioning Washington, and consumers would have lost warnings federal law does not currently require. The limited carve-outs for dating, pricing, and origin labels narrow but do not erase that loss [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Burr of North Carolina introduced the bill on August 3, 1998, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3].
It gathered 17 cosponsors in total — 11 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on August 17, 1998 [S5].
No further action was taken; there was no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers are better off: every state-level food warning and disclosure rule the bill would have wiped out remained in force. Food and beverage makers did not get the single national standard they sought, but they also avoided nothing — the status quo of state-by-state rules simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States kept their food warning powers

for.name: Reps. Greenwood, Upton, Ganske, Hall, Towns, and Strickland
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on August 17, 1998 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to subcommittee and never brought it before the full committee for a vote

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: the 17 cosponsors included 11 Republicans and 6 Democrats [S4], and opposition never had to organize because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced dozens of differing state warning rules with one federal standard, and would have eliminated state warnings federal law does not require — reducing labeling and disclosure costs the industry considers burdensome. Consumers lose the state warnings; the manufacturer saves the cost of giving them.

Retailers selling across state lines face the same patchwork of state labeling and warning rules; a single national standard would have simplified their compliance. Their gain comes at the cost of shoppers' access to state-mandated hazard warnings.
